stages.name: Question
stages.instructions:
Ask one answerable question, and say what you would do differently depending on the answer.

A question nobody would act on either way produces research nobody reads. If the answer would not change a decision, say which decision it would inform anyway — or do not file it.

Narrow beats broad: research against an unbounded question always returns something, and it is rarely what anyone wanted.

stages.name: Gather
stages.instructions:
Find out what is actually known, and bring back where you found it.

Read the question on the card and go looking. Prefer primary sources — the documentation, the code, the specification, the people who built the thing — over summaries of them. Where a claim matters, record where it came from; a fact with no source cannot be checked later and will be re-researched by somebody else.

**Attach every source as a reference.** A URL in prose is a hint; a reference is something the next stage and every later reader can open. Where a source is behind a login or is a local file, say so explicitly rather than attaching a link that will answer a login page to anyone who follows it.

Say what you could **not** find. A gap named is a finding; a gap passed over silently becomes a confident synthesis later built on nothing.

Hand off:
- `sources` — what you found, each with where it came from and how much weight it deserves
- `coverage` — what the question asked that you could not answer, and why

If the question is too broad to research, `block` and propose the narrower questions it should become. Research against an unbounded question returns something, and it is rarely the thing anybody wanted.

stages.name: Measure
stages.instructions:
Replace opinion with measurement wherever the question allows it.

Take the sources as given and go and get numbers: benchmarks, counts, timings, sizes, rates — whatever the question is actually about. Measure the real thing rather than a proxy for it, and when you must use a proxy, say that is what you did.

**A number without its method is not a measurement.** Record the tool, the version, the input, the environment and anything that would change the result. Somebody will try to reproduce this, and if they cannot, the number becomes an opinion with a decimal point.

Publish raw output where the reader can reach it and attach it as a reference. Summary tables are for reading; the raw data is what makes the summary checkable.

Hand off:
- `numbers` — the measurements, each one labelled with what it measures
- `method` — how, precisely enough to repeat

If nothing in the question can be measured, say so in `numbers` rather than measuring something adjacent because it was measurable. An honest "this is not a measurable question" is a real result and protects the synthesis from false precision.

stages.name: Synthesise
stages.instructions:
Answer the question that was asked, and say how sure you are.

Read the sources and the numbers and write what they add up to. Lead with the answer rather than the journey. Where the evidence is thin or the sources disagree, say so in the finding itself rather than in a caveat at the end that nobody reaches.

**Give a recommendation, not a menu.** A list of options with equal weight hands the work back to the person who asked. Say what you would do and why; name the strongest case against it so a reader can disagree on the merits.

State confidence honestly, and separately from the recommendation. `high` means the evidence would survive someone checking it; `low` means act on this only if the cost of being wrong is small. A confident recommendation on thin evidence is the most expensive thing this board can produce.

**Carrying the work onward.** If this leads to a change, the card that builds it lives on another board — set the same `projectId` on both and attach a reference to this card, because a `blocks` or `relates` link cannot cross boards. Without the shared project, the work arrives on the other board with none of this behind it.

Hand off:
- `findings` — what the evidence says, strongest first
- `recommendation` — what to do, and the best argument against it
- `confidence` — `high`, `medium` or `low`, and what would raise it

stages.name: Recommendation
stages.instructions:
Decide what to do with the answer.

Read the confidence before the recommendation. `low` confidence does not mean ignore it — it means act only if being wrong is cheap, and say so out loud if you act anyway.

If the recommendation leads to work, the work does not happen on this board. Create the card on the board that owns it, in the **same project**, with a reference back to this card. Research that ends at a recommendation nobody carried forward is the most expensive kind: it was done well and changed nothing.

stages.name: Filed
stages.instructions:
The question is answered and the answer is somewhere a person will find it later.

If the recommendation implied work and no card exists for it, say that here rather than letting `filed` imply the matter is closed.

cards.title: P4 exit test: one-paragraph synthesis of 'why the organization plane exists' (gate test — approve from Matrix)

artifactRouting.rule: Internal artifacts and all Guild work default to Atelier. Deliver product code, tests, migrations, assets and intended product documentation in the actual project repository only when this task calls for that delivery. Internal strategy about a public product stays private. Verify destination visibility and classification before any push/PR/issue/comment/attachment; never use public fallback. No secrets/raw private messages. Public promotion requires separate approval of exact sanitized material. Preserve gate/authority/merge boundaries.

P4 follow-up test: gate push reaches Matrix in seconds

spec.goal: Test card for the push-delivery fix (P4 follow-up). Write a two-sentence synthesis: 'Gates now reach Matrix by push within seconds; the 5-minute sweep remains the floor.' Do no research and use no tools. Complete immediately.
